note: Opened 2026-10-07: the county PDF itself (16 pages), 'Resolution No. 9-2022, Resolution of the Board of County Commissioners of Cherokee County Regulating and Licensing Industrial-Scale Wind Turbine Power Generation Facilities', 'PASSED and APPROVED by the Board of County Commissioners of Cherokee County, Kansas, this 3rd day of October, 2022', effective upon publication. The record's three values match: Sec. 3.C.4.a, 'a distance of 5250 feet between any turbine located in Cherokee County and the nearest property line'; Sec. 3.C.1, 'The maximum turbine height of any wind turbine shall not exceed four hundred forty (440) feet'; Sec. 3.C.3.a, no audible noise above '39 dBA ... during the hours of 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.' at any property line within 5250 feet of the nearest turbine. Differences from the record: it is a resolution, not an ordinance; the 39 dBA limit runs 10 p.m. to 7 a.m., not 'evening'. Night and day noise limits may be waived by a recorded agreement with all landowners within 5250 feet. Removed from the earlier note, which came from search-index text: that it was adopted unanimously and the reference to the commission minutes; the resolution read here shows the date but not the vote, and the minutes were not opened.

Opened 2026-10-08: City of Pasadena (Texas) City Council record of proceedings, regular meeting of January 7, 2025: public hearing 'on the extension of the Commercial Moratorium imposed by the City of Pasadena, Texas, on the issuance of permits for the placement and installation of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) Facilities', then 'ORDINANCE 2025-001 - Authorizing and approving the Extension of the Commercial Moratorium ... passed on second and final reading. MOTION CARRIED, UNANIMOUS.' Differences from the record: the extension is Ordinance 2025-001, adopted 2025-01-07; the minutes give no term or end date; the original 2024 ordinance number was not found. Pasadena City Council imposed a commercial moratorium on permits for BESS facilities (City and ETJ) by Ordinance 2024-198: public hearings and first reading 2024-10-01, second and final reading at the 2024-10-08 special meeting (minutes). The extension ordinance recites that the moratorium expires 90 days after adoption unless extended, and Section 2 extends it once for a 90-day period past January 6, 2025; council minutes show it as Ordinance 2025-001, first reading 2025-01-06 and final reading 2025-01-07, unanimous (a first reading on 2024-12-17 was deferred). By its own terms the extension ran out in early April 2025 (90 days past January 6, 2025). On 2025-04-01 the council passed on final reading Ordinance 2025-082 adding Chapter 9, Article XII, Energy Storage Systems (first reading 2025-03-18), a permanent land use code for BESS that does not mention the moratorium. I found no further extension or new BESS moratorium: council minutes from 2025-01-21 through 2025-07-01 and 2025-11-18 have no BESS item, and page 2 (docketed public hearings, which a Texas ch. 212 moratorium or extension requires) of every council agenda from June 2025 through October 2026 lists no BESS hearing. The record's status extended/in_force and its claim that the moratorium is active and expires October 2026 are contradicted; the moratorium appears to have expired in April 2025 and been superseded by Ordinance 2025-082. The text of Ordinance 2024-198 itself was not read (the October 1, 2024 backup packet is a 762-page scan with no text layer); its date, scope and 90-day term are taken from the October 2024 minutes and the recitals of Ordinance 2025-001. The extension text read is the agenda-backup copy (number left blank, dated 12/10/24); the minutes confirm adoption under the same caption. Quoted: "WHEREAS, that the moratorium imposed by the City of Pasadena on the issuance of permits for the placement and installation of BESS facilities within the City relates to the preservation of the public peace, health, safety, and/or welfare of the citizens and following its adoption will expire 90 days therefrom, unless extended prior to that date after notice and hearing; ... WHEREAS, the City of Pasadena after a public hearing held on January 6, 2025 and January 7, 2025 to hear residents and affected parties on the proposed extension of the moratorium imposed on October 8, 2024, finds that extending the moratorium for a 90 day period effective from January 7, 2025, is necessary ... SECTION 2. That the City Council finds it is in the best interest of the City and does hereby extend the commercial moratorium imposed on the issuance of permits for the placement and installation of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) facilities within the jurisdiction of the City of Pasadena, Texas as established by Ordinance 2024-198 for a 90-day period past January 6, 2025." Second reading (agent:blind-reviewer-8 (Claude Code, 2026-10-16), opened): The document is the City of Pasadena ordinance (2025-001) that extended the BESS commercial moratorium imposed October 8, 2024 by Ordinance 2024-198, for a 90-day period past January 6, 2025; the January 6, 2025 minutes record first reading and the January 7, 2025 minutes record passage on second and final reading. Read the text of Ordinance 2025-205 in the City of Pasadena's Agenda Backup Documents for the October 7, 2025 council meeting (PDF pages 434 to 474; unsigned first-reading copy with the number left blank; a scan with an OCR text layer, and the operative pages were checked against the page images). It amends the Fire Prevention Code (Chapter 13, Article VII, Secs. 13-151 and 13-152) to adopt the 2024 International Fire Code with local amendments, and Section 3 repeals Ordinance 2025-082 (adopted April 1, 2025) in whole (Section 6 only preserves rights and remedies already accrued to the City), because 'requirements regarding energy storage systems' are being updated in the fire code. Section 9 delays the whole ordinance until 90 days after council approval. The minutes printed in the October 21 and November 4, 2025 agendas show first reading on 2025-10-07 and second and final reading on 2025-10-21, both unanimous, with no amendment recorded; the October 21 backup does not reprint the text. The Fire Marshal's Plan Review page says the code was adopted October 21, 2025 and 'took effect January 19, 2026'. So Chapter 9 Article XII stayed in force until the repeal took effect on 2026-01-19 and has stood repealed since; the record's status active and currency in_force are out of date (a repealed instrument is recorded as lifted under COUNTY_CHECK section 3). Much of Article XII moved into a new IFC Section 1208 in Exhibit A. Section 1208.4 Site Location keeps the five-acre cap (now 'excluding setbacks areas'), 1,500 ft between BESS sites, 1,000 ft from critical facilities (redefined: hospitals, nursing homes, police and fire stations, utilities, hazardous-material sites, water and wastewater plants; schools, day care centers and government facilities, listed in 2025-082, are no longer named), 50 ft from the right of way, 150 ft from rear and side property lines (no longer limited to lines adjoining commercial property), no special flood hazard area, and frontage on a public right of way. Section 1208.3 still requires a Special Use Permit application and CenterPoint Energy review and approval before a city permit. Not carried over: the 500 ft setback from residential property, multifamily developments and manufactured home parks; the rule that a site lie within 150 ft of CenterPoint property; and the plume study. Section 1201.4 states land-use aims ('designation of properties suitable for the location' of a BESS; 'compatible land uses'), but the vehicle is the fire code, so whether Section 1208.4 counts under COUNTY_CHECK section 3 is a decision for the record-editor; its size cap and distances are local siting rules, not IFC clearances. No later council action on energy storage was found: the main council agendas from November 4, 2025 through October 6, 2026 (23 agendas, OCR'd here, carrying the minutes of the meetings before them) name no energy storage, battery, Article XII or Section 13-152 item, and AgendaCenter phrase searches after 2025-10-22 for energy storage, battery energy, fire code, Article XII, 13-152 and 1208 return no results (that index missed the October 7, 2025 backup, so it is not conclusive alone). Ordinance 2026-118 (final reading 2026-07-21) changes only the Section 13-12 fee schedule and names no BESS fee. Resolution 2026-11 (adopted April 7, 2026, effective immediately) replaces the county's wind regulations with amended Wind Energy Regulations in the Zoning Resolution, for wind facilities of 1 MW or more by special use permit in the Agricultural zone. Second reading (agent:blind-reviewer-14 (Claude Code, 2026-10-30), opened): The ordinance is the county's own wind siting rule and matches the record on height (600 ft), noise (32 dBA), flicker (none on non-participating residential property) and the 2,640 ft / 5x tip height setback from lot lines. The county's own copy of the Rural Zoning Code, opened as a PDF in this session, states a 160 ft maximum height and a 110% of blade-tip-height setback to all property lines for Large Wind Farms (5 MW or greater). The county's own current Development Code (revision dated October 21, 2026) states in 152.616(HHH)(6)(a)(3) a 2 mile setback from a turbine tower to a rural residence, measured from the tower centerline to the center point of the residence. The July 17, 2024 PDF named in data/review/nrel_restriction_conflicts.csv returned HTTP 404 and is now superseded by the October 2026 revision. Quoted: "(a) Setbacks. The minimum setback shall be a distance of not less than the following: (1) From a turbine tower to a city urban growth boundary (UGB) shall be two miles. ... (2) From turbine tower to land zoned Unincorporated Community (UC) shall be 1 mile. (3) From a turbine tower to a rural residence shall be 2 miles." The county's full ordinance PDF, opened and read in this session, sets a 3,520 foot wind turbine setback only for non-participating resource-zone dwellings (centerline to dwelling edge, or the DEQ noise distance if greater). The county's code publisher copy of Title 20 (March 21, 2024 edition) contains the commercial wind rules the NREL record appears to describe. Agreeing: the 400 ft total system height cap, and a property line setback equal to total system height (1x). Disagreeing: the record says setback from structures is 0 times tip height, but section 20.664.200.E sets 2,500 ft from master plan receiving areas and existing residences and 1,000 ft from public rights-of-way. Record omits: special use permit required for all commercial systems; commercial systems allowed only in FR-19 and FR-40 districts (use tables not read against district headings); blade diameter cap of 200 ft; noise compliance with chapter five of the 2006 Master Plan; wildlife species study within one mile; removal after one year of nonuse (120 days to remove). Small systems are separate: 90 ft cap, setback 2x total system height in agricultural, forest and range, and residential districts, 25 ft blade diameter cap, 5 gross acres per system. Only the 2024 edition was read; the county is rewriting Title 20 for planned adoption in 2026 (draft redline of April 2026 seen, definitions only, not the operative sections), so a newer text may differ. A commercial wind energy conversion system with a total system height more than 400 feet and that is intended to produce electricity to sell for consumption. A. A special use permit is required for all commercial wind energy conversion systems. B. Commercial wind energy conversion systems may be permitted in the FR-19 and FR-40 zoning districts. C. Total system height must not exceed 400 feet. D. The minimum setback for a property line which separates two distinct owners is equal to the total system height. E. The minimum setback from any master plan designated receiving area and any existing residence is 2,500 feet and 1,000 feet from any public right-of-way. F. The blade diameter must not exceed 200 feet." Second reading (agent:blind-reviewer-5 (Claude Code, 2026-11-08), opened): Section 20.664.200 of the Douglas County, Nevada code (copy stamped March 21, 2024) allows a commercial wind system only by special use permit in FR-19 and FR-40, caps total system height at 400 feet, and sets the property line setback at the total system height. The structures setback does not: the code requires 2,500 feet from any existing residence or master plan receiving area, and 1,000 feet from a public right-of-way, not 0 times tip height. Sec. 361-30 of the El Reno zoning code matches the record on the 600 ft total turbine height cap (variance available), the 55 dBA noise limit (measured at the exterior of an occupied building on a nonparticipating property, no hours) and the 1.1 times turbine height setback from nonparticipating property lines. The code also sets 1.1 times turbine height from public roads, third-party transmission lines and communication towers (the City may waive), and has shadow flicker, 50 ft rotor clearance, lighting and decommissioning provisions the record omits. Turbine height is measured to the highest rotor blade point. Wind facilities are by right in a Wind Energy Overlay district. Added 2011-08-02 by Ord. No. 9006; the copy read is an Internet Archive capture of 2024-07-25, so later amendments are not ruled out. Live ecode360 and Municode returned Cloudflare challenges. Quoted: "(b) Height restrictions. Total turbine height cannot exceed 600 feet without a variance from the Board of Adjustment. ... [1] Noise. [2] Nonparticipating landowner property lines. Wind turbines shall be set back a distance of at least 1.1 times the turbine height from adjacent nonparticipating landowner property lines. ... [3] Occupied buildings. Wind turbines shall be set back a distance of 1,000 feet from any occupied building. ... The owner of the occupied building may waive this setback requirement, but in no case shall a wind turbine be located closer to an occupied building than 1.1 times the turbine height." Second reading (agent:blind-reviewer-11 (Claude Code, 2026-11-08), archived): The El Reno code section sets a 600 foot total turbine height limit (variance available), a 55 dBA noise limit and setbacks, so the height limit, noise limit and property line setback in the record match. Live ecode360 returned HTTP 403; read the Internet Archive copy.

No. 383 of 2011-11-28 in the history note of Sec 109-120 only; the record gives no enactment date, and the code does not state a status or end date, so those fields were not compared. Property line. Three times its total height from the nearest property line unless mitigation has taken place and agreed by owner/operator and affected property owners involved and recorded in the county recorder's office [...] Public roads. 1.5, plus 100 feet times the total height from the nearest public road and right-of-way. The county's own posted scan of the ordinance adopted 13 June 2011 was read page by page as images (the PDF has no text layer). It confirms the 450 foot maximum height and the setback of 1.10 times tower height from adjacent property lines, with tower height measured to the highest blade point. It does not support the record's structure setback for non-participating owners: Section VI.H.1 sets 2000 feet from any Primary Structure, and 1.10 times tower height is only the floor that applies when the structure's owner waives the 2000 feet. An owner who has not waived keeps the 2000 feet, so the record's 1.1 times tip height understates the rule. This is the same point the two readers of 2026-10-28 differed on; this reading sides with 2000 feet as the rule for the field. The record also omits the 2000 foot setback from residential districts and the 1.10 times setback from public roads, third party transmission lines and communication towers. Status: the ordinance states no end date, and its closing clause reserves the Board's right to change or terminate it. A Brown County Board resolution of 10 May 2021, on the same page, recites that the ordinance was adopted 13 July 2009 and amended and adopted 13 June 2011 and names no later amendment. Nothing read here shows whether it was amended or repealed after May 2021, so the record's status of unknown is not settled. The 2009 version is posted beside it and was opened only at its signature page. Quoted: "H. Setbacks 1. All WECS Towers shall be set back at least 2000 feet from any Primary Structure. The distance for the above setback shall be measured from the point of the Primary Structure foundation closest to the WECS Tower to the center of the WECS Tower foundation. The owner of the Primary Structure may waive this setback requirement; but in no case shall a WECS Tower be located closer to a Primary Structure than 1.10 times the WECS Tower Height. All WECS Towers shall have a setback of 2000 feet from all residential districts. 2. All WECS Towers shall be set back a distance of at least 1.10 times the WECS Tower Height from public roads, third party transmission lines, and communication towers. [...] 3. All WECS Towers shall be set back a distance of at least 1.10 times the WECS Tower height from adjacent property lines. The affected adjacent property owner may waive this setback requirement. [...] K. HEIGHT All WECS facilities will have a maximum height not to exceed 450 feet." Second reading (agent:blind-reviewer-7 (Claude Code, 2026-11-11), opened): The PDF is the signed ordinance itself, a scan with no text layer, read from rendered page images. The 450 foot height limit (Section VI.K), the property line setback of 1.10 times tower height (VI.H.3) and the adoption year agree with the record; the full adoption date is June 13, 2011. WECS Tower Height is defined to the highest point of the rotor blade, so it is tip height. The record's setback from non-participating structures does not agree: Section VI.H.1 sets 2000 feet from any Primary Structure, and 1.10 times tower height applies only when the structure's owner waives the 2000 feet, which is the participating case. The ordinance also sets 2000 feet from residential districts and 1.10 times tower height from public roads, transmission lines and communication towers. This reading does not show whether the ordinance is still in force.

The county's own copy of Appendix A as revised on September 13, 2021 states every number in the record: a 500 foot tip height limit, a 40 Laeq noise limit, a setback of 2.64 times tip height or 1320 feet (whichever is greater), and a 2,250 foot setback. One field differs from the record in what the distance is measured from. The record gives 2,250 feet as a setback from non-participating structures. Section VI.L.1 measures the 2,250 feet to the nearest point of the property line of a non-participating parcel that has a primary structure, not to the structure itself. The number is the same and the rule is stricter than the record's label says. Owners may waive this setback, but never to less than 1,000 feet from the primary structure. Revised after the second reading on 2026-11-11: the first draft marked this field as agreeing and described the difference in the note; on re-reading Section VI.L.1 the measuring point is part of the value, so the field is marked as disagreeing. Three details go beyond the record. First, the 2.64 times or 1320 foot setback applies only to non-participating property lines without a primary structure. Second, the 40 Laeq limit applies at a primary structure between 9 P.M. and 6 A.M., and Illinois Pollution Control Board limits apply at the property line. Third, the document also bars towers within 1.5 miles of a municipality unless the municipality waives. The PDF does not carry a signed resolution page; the September 13, 2021 date comes from its cover and file name, and the 2023 amendment cites 'the text adopted by the Ford County Board on September 13, 2021' and lists that revision as RES 21-80. The record's status is unknown and this document does not settle it. A later instrument does bear on it: Resolution 23-49 (revised May 24, 2023, also opened in this session) replaces this text. It keeps the 500 foot limit but lets an FAA Determination of No Hazard set a greater height, keeps the 2,250 foot and 2.64 times setbacks with a fallback to the state statute's setbacks (2.1 times tip height from non-participating residences) if a court finds them invalid, and its noise section no longer contains the 40 Laeq limit (IPCB regulations only). Its sunset clause reinstates the 2021 text if Illinois courts find P.A. 102-1123 invalid. The live URL returned HTTP 404 to the second reader on 2026-10-28 and returned the PDF today. No later amendment or repeal was found: the township's ordinances page and site search list no later wind ordinance, and the nine text-readable 2021 supervisor minutes hold no wind ordinance action (the October and November 2021 minutes are scans and were not read; no January 2021 minutes are posted). The codified zoning ordinance on eCode360 could not be opened, so the current codified text was not checked.
